column3: It repeats the focus's Hell destination, recompense formula, and designation of its recipients as wrongdoers.
Its protection of a person responding to injustice offers only a distant justice and wrongdoing parallel.
The question about a theft penalty does not add to the focus's false-divinity claim or divine judgment.
The same recompense formula for beneficence provides a limited formal contrast to the focus's punitive use.
The nearby denial of purposeless creation supplies broad local setting but not the angelic claim or its penalty.
Divine reward for charity does not materially clarify punishment for claiming divinity.
Its explicit formula that God recompenses wrongdoers closely parallels the focus, despite the different offense.
It establishes that all in heaven and earth belong to God and that those near Him worship without pride.
Rewarding charitable efforts is too general after the more direct recompense parallels.
The recurring recompense formula for doers of good gives only a redundant formal contrast.
The immediately preceding distinction between God's unanswerability and creaturely accountability directly frames the focus's judgment.
It denies that beings invoked besides God can help themselves or their worshippers, directly undermining rival divinity.
It combines the lack of protectors besides God with a Hell destination, though it addresses guidance rather than a divinity claim.
The denial of authority over others helps distinguish unsupported claims from genuine sovereignty.
Its image of powerless protectors besides God reinforces the failure of alternatives to divine reliance.
It explicitly assigns Hell as a full recompense to those who follow Satan, providing a punitive counterpart.
The local repudiation of divine play contributes only remote setting for the focus's judicial warning.
Its statement of full recompense supports divine requital in general but adds no false-worship detail.
It combines Hell with God's formula for recompensing grave ingratitude, a close punitive pattern.
The tireless glorification of God continues the immediate portrait of the heavenly servants whom the focus warns.
Noah's rescue as recompense for one denied does not illuminate the focus's claim to divinity.
God's sufficiency and the futility of threats involving others directly weaken reliance on beings besides Him.
The nearby challenge to produce proof for gods besides God directly anticipates the focus's condemnation of such claims.
The absence of any protector or helper besides God is relevant but less specific than the direct rival-deity passages.
Its confession that none is deity but God and admission of wrongdoing provide a compact contrast to the focus's forbidden claim.
Its response to aggression adds little beyond the earlier human-justice parallel.
Reward for deeds gives no additional account of wrongful divine claims or Hell.
It states that no one can shelter the messenger from God and that no refuge exists besides Him.
The nearby overthrow of falsehood by truth supports the focus's repudiation of a false divine assertion.
Reward for faith and righteous works is too general to add after the stronger judgment passages.
The pledge to fill Hell with Satan and his followers supplies a direct image of punitive consequence.
Its argument that multiple gods would corrupt the cosmos directly rejects the premise that any other deity can exist.
Creation in truth and recompense without injustice give a theological account of the just judgment stated in the focus.
It records polytheists' attempted excuse for worship besides God and rejects their evasion through the messenger's clear delivery.
Proportionate human retaliation offers a limited justice-formula resonance but not the focus's divine judgment.
God's cosmic rule and the inability of those invoked besides Him to possess even a small thing directly negate rival sovereignty.
The warning about political alliances does not materially address divinity claims or their recompense.
The immediate challenge asks whether earth-born gods can raise the dead, directly exposing their incapacity.
The repeated reward formula for beneficence adds no meaningful value after earlier instances.
The challenge to show what beings besides God created directly tests and refutes any claim to divine status.
The immediate declaration that there is no deity but God and that He alone is to be worshipped states the focus's governing rule.
Its formula for the recompense of disbelievers supplies only a broad punitive parallel.
The demonstrative wording has no substantive relation to the focus's claim or judgment.
It associates wrongful oppression with a painful punishment, supporting the focus's classification of the claim as wrongdoing.
Another good-deed recompense formula is redundant and does not clarify the focus.
The exclusion of wrongdoers from God's covenant offers only an indirect contrast with usurped authority.
It corrects the claim that the Merciful has a child by identifying the beings at issue as honored servants.
It commands following revelation rather than taking protectors besides God, reinforcing exclusive allegiance.
The difficult Day is too unspecific to add to the focus's stated offense and penalty.
The servants' refusal to precede God in speech and their obedience to His command directly counter a claim to independent deity.
The maxim about rewarding excellence is a remote positive contrast with no added explanatory force.
Its prophetic call to worship God alone and reject any other deity supports the focus's exclusive-divinity premise.
Wrongdoers' denial of evil at death offers a general accountability scene without the false-divinity issue.
God's stated recompense of the ungrateful supplies a close formulaic example of punitive requital.
The call to worship God alone, with no other deity, and warning of a great Day supports the focus's premise and consequence.
God's knowledge, conditional permission for intercession, and the servants' fear immediately precede and explain the focus's warning.
Recompense according to deeds gives only a general judgment principle already well represented.
It rejects a plurality claim, affirms one deity, and warns its persistent proponents of painful punishment.
Reward for the God-conscious does not add to the focus's punitive analysis.
Reward for patience is unrelated to false divinity or its judgment.
The repeated call to worship God alone and warning of an encompassing Day reinforces the focus's exclusive-worship premise.
Its demand that the condemned be questioned offers a general accountability parallel after the direct local verse.
It links wrongdoing, rejected clear messengers, destruction, and God's recompense of criminals.
It explicitly states God's recompense for excess and disbelief in His signs, with a lasting afterlife punishment.
The expected acknowledgment that the earth belongs to God supports the sovereignty denied by a rival divinity claim.
It condemns invoking besides God what can neither harm nor benefit, directly exposing the futility of such worship.
Hell enclosing disbelievers is a broad punishment image without the focus's offense.
Its question about ownership of the earth and all within it reinforces God's exclusive sovereignty.
Reward for good deeds is not materially useful for the focus's wrongful-claim judgment.
It assigns Fire to deliberate transgression and wrongdoing, supporting the focus's punitive classification.
Human conflict resolution and equity do not add to divine sovereignty or false-divinity judgment.
It joins false protectors besides God with the failure of all defenses before Hell.
Turning from God's signs is named as the height of wrongdoing and met with divine retribution.
The condemned people's mutual accusation does not clarify divine or creaturely authority.
It confirms an additional punishment for wrongdoers, though it does not identify the specific wrong.
It directly addresses calling upon another deity without proof and places the claimant's account before God.
The assertion that truth has come while the opponents lie reinforces the focus's treatment of the claim as false.
Universal recompense according to acquisition and the absence of injustice state the just judgment principle behind the focus.
It connects arrogant refusal of God's worship with entry into Hell, closely paralleling the focus's proud divine claim.
Dismissing an old promise as ancient tales does not add to the focus's deity claim or recompense.
It joins recompense for evil with the absence of any protector or helper besides God.
It explicitly calls the Fire the recompense of wrongdoers, closely echoing the focus's final clause.
Truth's independence from human desire, cosmic order, and rejected reminder provide a broader anti-falsehood setting.
It criticizes worship besides God, rejects alleged intercessory knowledge, and declares God's transcendence over association.
Hell surrounding disbelievers is a generic consequence already supplied more specifically elsewhere.
God's knowledge and wisdom alone add no focused account of the claim or its punishment.
Its eventual recompense according to acquisition is a general judicial parallel only.
The formula for recompensing gratitude gives a limited formal contrast to the focus's recompense of wrongdoing.
God's possession of all dominion and unequaled power to protect directly reinforce His unique sovereignty.
It asks why people worship besides God what has no power to harm or benefit, directly denying rivals' divine capacity.
Bearing a burden on the Day of Resurrection supplies only a general consequence for turning away.
Its statement of recompense for deeds is too general after the direct punishment formulations.
The repayment of a favor does not clarify divine judgment for a false deity claim.
Reward for righteous works is not useful to the focus's punitive and exclusive-worship argument.
The instruction not to assert a future action has no material relation to claiming divinity.
The division between righteous and lesser groups does not clarify the focus's divine claim or Hell.
The description of a drink's mixture has no relevant connection.
Its challenge to claimed special closeness to God offers a distant parallel to an unsupported elevated claim.
Revelation, judgment by God's book, and disbelief in its rejection provide only an indirect authority and accountability parallel.
It describes equal recompense for evil, the lack of protection from God, and abiding in the Fire.
It rejects any prophetic claim that people should worship the messenger instead of God, directly bounding creaturely status.
It specifically rejects taking angels or prophets as lords, making it an especially close corrective to the focus's angel context.
It rejects exaggeration about the Messiah and the claim of three, while affirming God's oneness.
It condemns the claim that the Messiah is God and explicitly assigns the Fire as the associate's destination.
God questions Jesus about telling people to take him and his mother as gods besides God, directly testing a creaturely divinity claim.
It describes associating the jinn with God and fabricating children for Him, a close parallel to false claims about heavenly beings.
It asks whether partners are attributed to God even though they create nothing and are themselves created.
Those near the Lord are not too proud for His worship and prostrate to Him, closely paralleling the immediate angelic setting.
Every creature, including the angels, prostrates to God without arrogance, directly reinforcing their servanthood.
It forbids taking two gods and declares that God alone is one God.
Its hypothetical rival gods would seek a way against the Lord of the Throne, exposing their dependence rather than divinity.
It denies that God has a child, a partner in dominion, or a protecting ally, directly rejecting the theological premises surrounding the focus.
It joins taking gods besides God to the demand for clear authority and calls unsupported fabrication the greatest wrongdoing.
It identifies taking gods besides God for honor as the false reliance whose reversal follows in the next verse.
The supposed gods will deny their worship and become opponents, directly overturning false divine allegiance.
It records the false assertion that the calf was the people's and Musa's god, furnishing an explicit instance of a creaturely divinity claim.
It declares that God alone is deity and encompasses all things in knowledge, directly answering the false claim in the preceding passage.
It challenges beings invoked besides God by their inability even to create a fly or recover what it takes.
It rejects both divine offspring and any other deity, arguing that multiple gods would yield competing dominion.
It exalts God as the true King and declares that there is no deity but Him.
It describes supposed gods besides God as created beings with no power over death, life, or resurrection.
It combines God's creative and providential acts with the challenge to produce proof for a deity alongside Him.
It forbids calling on another deity with God and affirms that all authority and final return belong to Him.
Those called besides God do not possess even an atom's weight in the heavens or earth and have no share or support.
God's question to the angels about whether people worshipped them directly addresses misdirected worship of heavenly servants.
The angels deny such worship and identify the jinn as the actual objects of many people's belief.
Those invoked besides God cannot answer and will deny their associates' worship on the Day of Resurrection.
It rejects taking gods besides the Merciful because their intercession and rescue are powerless before His harm.
Its declaration that the deity is one gives a concise direct statement of the focus's exclusive-divinity premise.
It contrasts God's acknowledged creation of heaven and earth with the powerlessness of beings called besides Him.
It assigns all intercession to God, closely supporting the focus passage's preceding restriction of angelic intercession.
It identifies the condemned response: disbelief when God alone was invoked and belief when partners were associated with Him.
It reproves the designation of the Merciful's servants, the angels, as female and warns that this claim will be recorded and questioned.
It declares that He alone is God in heaven and God on earth, confirming universal and exclusive divinity.
It challenges those who invoke others besides God to show what they created or what revealed authority supports them.
It limits even the angels' intercession to God's permission and pleasure, reinforcing their subordinate status.
It condemns those who deny the Hereafter for naming the angels with female names, closely matching the local polemic about angelic beings.
It commands that places of worship belong to God and that no one be invoked alongside Him.
The messenger declares that he calls only upon his Lord and associates no one with Him.
Its declaration of God's absolute oneness gives the most concise doctrinal statement opposed to any rival deity claim.
It denies that God begets or is begotten, directly rebutting the false filial theology corrected in the focus's immediate context.
It calls for worship of God alone and rejects taking one another as lords besides Him.
It treats associating partners with God as the grave sin that is not forgiven without repentance.
It repeats the warning that association with God is an unforgiven and far-straying error.
It condemns the explicit claim that the Messiah, son of Mary, is God and affirms God's unrestricted power.
It forbids associating with God anything for which He has sent down no authority, matching the focus's unsupported claim.
Those invoked besides God are identified as servants like their callers, directly denying independent divinity.
It records the claims that Ezra or the Messiah is God's son and identifies them as imitation of prior disbelief.
It condemns taking religious authorities and the Messiah as lords besides God rather than worshipping the one God.
On the Day of Judgment, God separates the associates from their worshippers and confronts their claimed partnership.
It contrasts many competing lords with the one, irresistible God.
It challenges the attribution of partners who create nothing and are created, while affirming God as Creator of all things.
Those invoked besides God create nothing and are themselves created.
The supposed gods are dead, not living, and do not know when they will be resurrected.
It affirms one God and identifies refusal of that truth with arrogant hearts.
God asks the associates where their alleged partners are on the Day of Resurrection.
Those called besides God cannot remove or transfer harm, directly denying their divine efficacy.
The beings whom people invoke themselves seek nearness to their Lord and fear His punishment.
The calf cannot speak, harm, or benefit, explicitly demonstrating the impotence of the false god claim.
Harun tells the people that the calf is a trial and that the Merciful alone is their God.
It declares God the true reality and whatever is invoked besides Him false, while affirming His supremacy.
It condemns worshipping besides God what lacks both revealed authority and knowledge.
God questions those worshipped besides Him about whether they led His servants astray, making false worship answerable.
It notes worship of what neither benefits nor harms besides God, a concise parallel to false dependence.
After God's creative provision, it asks whether there is a deity alongside God and exposes the false equation.
God calls the alleged partners on the Day of Judgment and asks where they are.
The alleged partners are summoned and challenged to guide, while the truth of their false association becomes manifest.
God again calls the alleged partners and asks for proof of their claim.
It identifies worship besides God as worship of idols and fabricated falsehoods, while provision belongs to God alone.
Luqman calls associating partners with God a tremendous wrongdoing, directly clarifying the focus's final designation.
It restricts intercession before God to His permission, reinforcing the limited standing of all heavenly beings.
It asks whether any creator besides God provides from heaven and earth, then declares there is no deity but Him.
It describes people taking gods besides God in hope of help, setting up their demonstrated inability to help.
It recounts arrogant refusal when people were told that there is no deity except God.
It states the objection to abandoning supposed gods for a messenger, directly displaying resistance to exclusive worship.
It records the objection to making all gods into one God, a direct articulation of polytheistic resistance.
It declares that there is no deity but the one, overpowering God.
It requires worship to be devoted purely to God and rejects treating others as protectors who supposedly bring people near to Him.
It rejects the assertion that God has taken a child and affirms His absolute oneness and dominance.
It describes those who recoil when God alone is mentioned yet rejoice when others are named with Him.
It rejects being called to disbelieve in God and associate with Him what has no knowledge-based warrant.
The alleged partners besides God are summoned for account, and their worshippers admit their disappearance.
It states that the God is one and commands upright devotion to Him.
It challenges whether any deity besides the Merciful was appointed for worship through prior messengers.
It exposes the person who takes personal desire as a god, extending the focus's critique to a false internal authority.
It calls those who invoke beings besides God that cannot answer until the Day of Resurrection the farthest astray.
It forbids setting up another deity alongside God and warns of the clear admonition.
It begins the critique of the named goddesses whose status is later exposed as unsupported conjecture.
It denies that the named supposed gods are anything but names without divine authority, following desire rather than guidance.
The messenger declares he has no independent power to harm or benefit, directly contrasting creaturely limitation with divinity.
It identifies God as the self-sufficient refuge, a positive statement of the independence denied to all alleged rivals.
It denies that anything is comparable to God, ruling out a peer capable of sharing divinity.
